html:
The iron pillar of Delhi is a column of wrought iron about 7.2 metres high, standing in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli in Delhi. It was made around 400, in the Gupta age, and it has hardly rusted in some 1,600 years.

A Sanskrit inscription says it was raised as a standard of the god Vishnu by a king named Chandra, usually identified with Chandragupta II. It probably stood first elsewhere, perhaps in central India, and was moved to Delhi centuries later, possibly in the 11th century or under the Delhi Sultanate, whose builders put up the Qutb Minar and mosque beside it.

It was forged from many pieces of hot iron hammered together, a huge feat for the time. Its resistance to rust comes from the iron's high phosphorus content and the way it was made: a thin protective film, rich in iron, oxygen and phosphorus, formed on its surface. Delhi's fairly dry climate also helps.

The pillar shows the skill of ancient Indian metal workers, later known abroad for wootz steel.
